CHIEF COMPLAINT
Upper respiratory symptoms: fatigue and shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrew is a 59-year-old male with a past medical history significant for depression, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension who presents with an upper respiratory infection.

Over the past week or so, he has felt very tired and short of breath after doing yard work. He believes he caught his first cold, since he has been wearing masks less at the end of the summer, and feels it has worsened. He has had both COVID vaccines. He has no history of seasonal allergies.

Dyspnea occurs mainly with exertion, such as lifting or carrying heavy bags of soil while landscaping, and he became very winded. He has no cough yet but feels it may be coming. He felt a little warm but attributed this to exertion. He reports elbow pain and tired knees with some tension around the knees, which he attributes largely to lifting the bags. He denies nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

Depression: It has been a stressful year and a half, but he reports doing well for the most part. His wife got him into barre classes to help him relax, and he feels they are helping. He previously discussed with the physician not starting medication for depression because he takes medications for other conditions.

Type 2 diabetes: He monitors his blood glucose on workdays but usually forgets on weekends. Diet has been good for the most part except for occasional house parties. His sugars have not been elevated during this illness.

Hypertension: He monitors his blood pressure regularly on workdays but not as consistently on weekends. He reports it has been under control. He is taking his medication. He needs a refill of lisinopril.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue. Felt warm, no measured fever.
Respiratory: Positive for exertional shortness of breath. No cough yet.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for elbow pain and knee tiredness/tension.
Psychiatric: Depression stable.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Depression
Type 2 diabetes
Hypertension

MEDICATIONS
Metformin
Lisinopril 20 mg daily

ALLERGIES
No history of seasonal allergies.

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Normal. Afebrile.
Cardiovascular: Heart sounds strong.
Respiratory: Scattered rhonchi bilaterally that clear with cough.
Musculoskeletal: Pain to palpation of bilateral elbows.
Extremities: Mild edema of the lower extremities.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: No airspace disease, no pneumonia.
Hemoglobin A1c: 8, mildly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Upper respiratory infection, likely viral syndrome
- Send COVID test to confirm negative; COVID is not suspected given no known exposures.
- Expected to resolve in a couple of days.
- Robitussin for cough.
- Ibuprofen or Tylenol for fever.
- Return if symptoms worsen.

2. Depression
- Doing well with current management, including barre classes.
- Offered medication or referral to psychotherapy; patient declined for now and may revisit in a few months.

3. Type 2 diabetes
- Hemoglobin A1c is 8; goal is 6 to 7.
- Increase metformin to 1000 mg twice daily.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in 4 months (ordered).

4. Hypertension
- Well controlled.
- Continue lisinopril 20 mg daily; refill ordered.
- Order lipid panel.

Follow-up in about 4 months; the nurse will assist with scheduling.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Annual exam.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Andrea is a 52-year-old female with a past medical history significant for rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and reflux who presents today for her annual exam. It has been one year since her last visit.

Rheumatoid arthritis: She has been walking, exercising, and doing yoga as previously advised. She reports that the constant movement has helped her arthritis significantly. She has had no joint pain, stiffness, or flare-ups over the past year. She continues to take methotrexate once weekly without any issues.

Atrial fibrillation: She has been going in and out of atrial fibrillation over the past year or so. She continues to have palpitations, most recently about a week ago. She notes that palpitations flare up when she becomes stressed. She has tried meditation and running with her dog to relieve stress, without much benefit. She called last month, and an event monitor was placed.

Reflux: She was started on Protonix and planned dietary modifications. She has cut out soda, which seems to have helped, and the medication has also been helping. She has not had a flare-up in about five months.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No complaints noted.
HEENT: Positive for nasal congestion due to allergies.
Cardiovascular: Positive for palpitations. Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea or vomiting.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or stiffness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Rheumatoid arthritis
Atrial fibrillation
Reflux

MEDICATIONS
Methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly
Protonix (pantoprazole) 40 mg daily

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Reviewed. Heart rate well controlled.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, previously noted and unchanged.
Respiratory: Lungs clear.
Musculoskeletal: Right elbow with edema and erythema, and pain to palpation.
Extremities: No lower extremity edema.

RESULTS
Event monitor: Shows the patient going in and out of atrial fibrillation with a conversion pause (pause in atrial fibrillation followed by return to regular rhythm).

Autoimmune panel: Within normal limits, consistent with well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Rheumatoid arthritis
- Well controlled on methotrexate, and autoimmune panel is reassuring.
- Continue methotrexate 2.5 mg once weekly. Refill ordered.
- Referral back to rheumatology is available if needed, but she appears stable.

2. Atrial fibrillation
- Paroxysmal, with ongoing palpitations triggered by stress. Event monitor shows episodes of atrial fibrillation with a conversion pause.
- The goal is to maintain normal sinus rhythm. Given her age and the intermittent nature of her atrial fibrillation, cardiac ablation is recommended.
- Referral placed to cardiology for cardiac ablation. The procedure was explained as mapping where the rhythm originates and ablating that area to prevent recurrence.

3. Reflux
- Well controlled, with no flare-ups in about five months.
- Continue Protonix 40 mg daily.
- Continue dietary modifications, including avoiding coffee and spicy foods.
- She will notify the office if she has any further issues.

Emergency room follow-up for hyperglycemia.

During that time he and his wife were eating cafeteria and fast food. His mother is feeling better now. He felt much better after returning home from the ER visit and reports he has been following his diet closely since then. Before this episode, his diet was consistent during the week because he is busy, but less consistent on weekends when he is socializing and having people over.

Kidney transplant: He reports being diligent with his immunosuppressive medications. He saw Dr. Reyes about 3 weeks ago, and kidney function was good at that time.

Depression: He reports the past year and a half has been tough, but he is doing pretty well. He has occasional difficult moments but does well if he has time to relax in the afternoon. He previously discussed with the doctor holding off on medication because of his many other medications. He prefers to avoid therapy at this time. His wife recently got him into meditation, which he finds relaxing, and he would like to continue it for a couple more months.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain.
Respiratory: Denies shortness of breath.
Neurological: Denies lightheadedness and dizziness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Depression
Type 2 diabetes
Kidney transplant

MEDICATIONS
Lantus (insulin glargine), dose prior to today's visit not specified
Immunosuppressive medications (managed by Dr. Reyes)

Hemoglobin A1c: approximately 8, mildly elevated.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hyperglycemia / type 2 diabetes
- Recent ER visit for elevated blood sugar, likely related to dietary indiscretion during his mother's hospitalization. Hemoglobin A1c is approximately 8, indicating blood sugars have been somewhat elevated beyond that one day.
- Increase Lantus to 20 units at night.
- Continue monitoring blood sugars and notify the office of readings, as further adjustment may be needed.
- Repeat hemoglobin A1c in a couple of months (ordered).

2. Depression
- Doing well with current strategies, including meditation.
- Hold off on medication or therapy at this time.
- Patient to call if he needs anything.

3. Kidney transplant
- Kidney function stable.
- Patient to follow up with Dr. Reyes to manage all immunosuppression medications. Dr. Reyes will contact this provider if needed.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

Symptoms have been present for about 10 days. He has noticed some swelling, including mild swelling in his legs, and feels lethargic. He attributes this partly to attending house parties and eating salty foods. He becomes short of breath when walking up a flight of stairs. He is a little uncomfortable and stiff when waking in the morning, and it takes him a while to adjust to walking after getting up. He had one episode of waking acutely short of breath at night about a week ago and none since.

Type 1 diabetes: He uses an insulin pump. He monitors his blood sugars during the work week but often forgets on Saturdays and Sundays because he is busy. He has not noticed any spikes. He admits to enjoying chocolate bars.

Depression: He reports a "crazy year and a half." He tried natural approaches, including outdoor stretching every morning in the summer, but the weather has changed and he needs alternatives. He is not ready to try medications and is open to suggestions. He denies any thoughts of harming himself or others.

Reflux: He is on omeprazole and has been making lifestyle modifications, including cutting back on Red Bull and caffeine. Alcohol intake has been difficult to limit during the holiday season, but he reports he is better.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for lethargy. Negative for fever or chills.
Cardiovascular: Positive for leg swelling. Negative for chest pain.
Respiratory: Positive for shortness of breath on exertion. Negative for cough.
Gastrointestinal: Negative for abdominal pain.
Psychiatric: Positive for depression. Negative for suicidal or homicidal ideation.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Type 1 diabetes
Congestive heart failure
Depression
Reflux

MEDICATIONS
Insulin pump
Omeprazole

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Within normal limits, including oxygen saturation at rest.
Neck: No jugular venous distension. No carotid bruits.
Cardiovascular: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur.

Extremities: 1+ pitting edema in the lower extremities.

RESULTS
Chest x-ray: No evidence of airspace disease.
Labs: No elevated white blood cell count.

1. Shortness of breath, acute heart failure exacerbation
- Likely fluid retention related to dietary indiscretion. Exam shows bibasilar crackles and 1+ pitting edema. Chest x-ray shows no airspace disease or pneumonia, and the normal white blood cell count makes infection unlikely.
- Start Lasix 40 mg daily.
- Weigh himself daily. Call if weight is not decreasing or is increasing.
- Call the office if shortness of breath worsens. If he becomes more short of breath at rest, call 911 and go to the emergency room, as he may need intravenous diuretics.

2. Type 1 diabetes
- Order hemoglobin A1c in about one month to determine whether any adjustments are needed.
- Follow up with endocrinologist.
- Ensure a recent eye exam.

3. Depression
- Refer to psychiatry for talk therapy.
- No medications at this time, per patient preference.

4. Reflux
- Continue omeprazole 20 mg daily.

The patient had no questions at the end of the visit and was instructed to call with any breathing problems.
